items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Humans exhibit a near‐universal right‐handed bias, linked to hemispheric brain lateralization, yet its evolutionary origins remain unclear. Wild chimpanzees, one of our closest living relatives, show diverse tool‐use behaviors and substantial variability, providing an appropriate context to investigate the emergence and functional significance of handedness in ecologically relevant settings. This study aimed to assess chimpanzee handedness and grip at both the individual and behavioral levels to determine whether specific tool‐use tasks elicit consistent preferences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We investigated hand preferences and grasping patterns in wild chimpanzees for three tool‐use behaviors observed in three different communities: accumulative stone throwing, algae fishing, and nut cracking. Our dataset consisted of camera‐trap videos of unhabituated wild chimpanzees with individuals identified across videos.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found 20/21 individual chimpanzees were consistent in their hand preference during primary tool‐use actions: fishing, hammering, or throwing. Insufficient observations of a further 16 chimpanzees prevented assessment of their hand preference. We found no evidence for behavior‐ or population‐level biases in hand preference. Grips were only possible to code for algae fishing, where we found pronounced inter‐individual variability in grasping, with notable trends between left‐ and right‐handed chimpanzees. Also, right‐handed individuals appeared to fish for longer durations, although the implications for tool‐use performance remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlights challenges and complexity associated with plant‐based precision‐grasping tool‐use behaviors like algae fishing. During the early stages of hominin evolution, the efficient execution of such manual behaviors likely benefited from key evolutionary adaptations favoring improved dexterity, motor skills, and enhanced brain‐hand coordination.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Ammie K. Kalan, Mimi Arandjelovic, Hjalmar Kuehl, Skye Bartel‐Ens, Amy Christensen, Julia Whelan, Anthony Agbor, Paula Dieguez, Juan Lapuente, Amelia C. Meier, Fotios Alexandros Karakostis

items.abstract: <jats:p>This special volume emphasises the need to integrate different lines of evidence to understand the effects of human activities on landscapes within the framework of the Anthropocene. The accelerated deterioration of animal and plant communities in recent times makes it a great challenge to find modern analogues that best fits as a baseline in paleoenvironmental and palaeoecological reconstructions. Studies included here evaluated and discussed the evidence about changes in mammals communities in different environments of Argentina induced by human activities, focussing particularly in recent times (post-Hispanic), although some of them also evaluated the relation between humans and the environment in the last 1600 yr. Different sources and proxy data were employed in the analysis: (1) fossil and subfossil sequences of small mammals, (2) stable isotopic analyses and (3) mammal specimens deposited in museums and biological collections.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Archaeologists have devoted a significant amount of effort to define their types, or units of analysis. However, strong disagreements persist even after years of debate. This may occur for many reasons, some intrinsic to the archaeological record itself—since different technocomplexes may involve distinct and not always comparable types—and others related to the discipline’s epistemology, where interobserver bias and differences in theoretical schools and training traditions can play a key role. As a result, most archaeological analyses, usually based on type presence/absence or type frequencies, present uncertainty levels from the start, which are not always due to the archaeological record itself, but to how we analyse that record. In this work, we adopt a materialist view to present an alternative approach where we analyse purely artefact shape without the need for previous categorisation. To do this, we resort to Geometric Morphometrics, widely used in archaeology, and we develop a simulation framework for stepwise artefactual change. We provide the software tools to do this, which have been compiled in the R-package Simumorph, and we showcase its performance in four simulated archaeological scenarios. Here, we base our simulations on the geometric microliths found during the Early and Middle Holocene in the Western Mediterranean, but the framework can be applied to any context where shape variation matters.</jats:p>
items.summary: 《模拟物质文化中的形状变异：Simumorph R包》：该研究提出无需预先分类、直接分析器物形状的替代路径，基于几何形态测量学开发了逐步器物变化的模拟框架，并打包为Simumorph R包，在西地中海早中全新世几何细石器的四个模拟考古场景中展示其表现，适用于任何关注形状变异的情境，值得考古学与几何形态测量学研究者阅读。
items.title: Simulating Shape Variation in Material Culture: The Simumorph R-package
items.venue: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>When in energetically demanding environments (e.g., high altitude, backcountry expeditions), humans acclimatize to compounded intensive stressors. Acclimatization is possible in part by using the dynamically responsive neuroendocrine system, with changes to hormones like cortisol (CORT) and testosterone (T), which both play important metabolic roles. We sought to examine how these hormones change during acclimatization and what their relationship was to energetic outcomes (i.e., physical activity intensity and average energy expenditure (AEE)).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected from 70 healthy individuals (age range: 18–53 years; female = 39) throughout a 3‐month long expedition in the American Rockies. Repeated measures of pre‐activity salivary baseline and acute change (i.e., reactivity) samples of CORT and T were taken throughout the 3‐month period. Physical activity intensity and energy expenditure were also assessed in a subset of participants using the wGT3X‐BT Actigraph monitor.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over the 3‐month period, we found that time on the course moderated the relationship between CORT reactivity and physical activity intensity (%MVPA) and AEE. Compared to the start of the expedition, female baseline T was significantly higher in the middle and end, and male baseline T was significantly higher at the end. Additionally, female T acutely declined significantly more at the end of the expedition compared to the beginning. We also found that time on course and sex moderated the relationship between T reactivity and activity intensity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest a dynamic relationship between neuroendocrine and energetic outcomes during acclimatization, which may further differ between sexes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Mallika S. Sarma, Cara J. Ocobock, Shannon Rochelle, Sarah Martin, Shalender Bhasin, Clare Super, S. Finn Warrick, Lee T. Gettler

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The intestinal epithelial barrier is anatomically and functionally distinct and specifically refers to the barrier formed by epithelial cells (enterocytes) and associated junctional complexes (tight junctions, adherens junctions, and desmosomes). The junctional complex is composed of specialized junctional proteins that regulate nutrient permeability across the gut epithelium while preventing passage of antigens, bacteria, and toxins. Modifying the junctional protein expression and disrupting the junctional complex structure result in intestinal hyperpermeability, referred to as “leaky gut.” The leakiness promotes endotoxemia and systemic inflammation, which orchestrate metabolic diseases of multiple organs, notably the liver. Ethanol and its metabolite acetaldehyde, bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) deliver a four‐pronged attack disrupting the gut epithelial barrier in alcohol use disorder (AUD). This article reviews the benefits of protecting the gut epithelial barrier structure and function in AUD. Adequate nutritional support is essential for maintaining the barrier integrity and sustaining gut health. Dietary nutrients and biotics supplements are effective in reinforcing the gut epithelial barrier integrity. Accordingly, this article elaborates on the prominent roles of dietary zinc, glutamine, and vitamin D supplementation in modulating the gut barrier junctional protein expression while mitigating the epithelial barrier breakdown induced by ethanol, acetaldehyde, LPS, and NETs. The efficacy of prebiotics, probiotics, and postbiotics in preventing disruption of the gut epithelial barrier in AUD is also reviewed. In summary, dietary nutrients and biotics supplements are beneficial in preserving the gut epithelial barrier integrity in AUD, thereby offering a supportive treatment option for alcohol‐related diseases.</jats:p>
authors: Ki M. Mak, Aditya C. Shekhar
